lesson.title: The Reciprocal Rule: dx/dy Meets dy/dx
lesson.summary: In Leibniz notation the Inverse Function Theorem becomes dy/dx = 1/(dx/dy), a compact reciprocal relationship you can apply with a short, repeatable four-step routine.
lesson.body:
The Inverse Function Theorem has a compact Leibniz-notation form that is worth memorizing as its own formula. If y = f^{-1}(x), which is the same as saying x = f(y), then dy/dx = 1/(dx/dy). In words, the derivative of the inverse function is the reciprocal of the derivative of the original function, with the two derivatives evaluated at corresponding points, one measured in terms of x and the other in terms of y.

A repeatable four-step routine applies this cleanly. Step one: identify a point a with known output b = f(a). Step two: compute f'(a), which plays the role of dx/dy at the corresponding y-value. Step three: take the reciprocal. Step four: that reciprocal is (f^{-1})'(b), the value of dy/dx at x = b.

Apply it to f(x) = 2x^3 + 1. Here f'(x) = 6x^2. At x = 1, f(1) = 2(1) + 1 = 3, and f'(1) = 6(1) = 6. So (f^{-1})'(3) = 1/6. Because this particular cubic is easy to invert, you can verify the answer directly. Solve y = 2x^3 + 1 for x: x^3 = (y - 1)/2, so x = [(y - 1)/2]^{1/3}. Differentiate with respect to y: dx/dy = (1/3)[(y - 1)/2]^{-2/3} (1/2) = (1/6)[(y - 1)/2]^{-2/3}. At y = 3, (y - 1)/2 = 1, and 1 raised to any power is still 1, so dx/dy = 1/6, matching the reciprocal shortcut exactly.

This kind of double check, computing the same derivative both by the reciprocal formula and by explicit inversion whenever explicit inversion happens to be possible, is a good habit whenever you are first getting comfortable with the formula. Once it feels automatic, you can rely on it in the more common situation, like the previous chapter's cubic-plus-linear example, where explicit inversion is not an option at all.
